claims.title: Bantu peoples settle the region
claims.summary: Bantu-speaking farmers and ironworkers settled the forests and savannas of the modern Congo over the first millennium CE, founding the Kongo, Teke, Vili, Mboshi and other communities that make up the country's peoples.

claims.title: Rise of the Kingdom of Loango
claims.summary: The Vili built the Kingdom of Loango on the Atlantic coast, with its capital at Buali; ruled by the maloango, it became a producer of cloth and a centre of trade in copper, ivory and enslaved people.

claims.title: The Teke (Anziku) kingdom inland
claims.summary: North of the Congo River the Teke (Bateke), organised as the Anziku or Tio kingdom under a sacred king titled the makoko, controlled the interior plateaus and trade routes; the northern reaches of Kongo also touched the region.

sources.label: History of the Republic of the Congo

claims.title: Loango becomes a hub of the Atlantic trade
claims.summary: The Loango coast, with markets at Loango Bay, Malemba and Cabinda, grew into a major export point for ivory, copper and enslaved people; Vili middlemen linked interior caravan networks to European ships offshore.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1650-loango-becomes-a-hub-of-the-atlantic-trade, claim TL:COG:event:1650:loango-becomes-a-hub-of-the-atlantic-trade, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Peak of the slave trade through Loango
claims.summary: By the eighteenth century the Loango ports were embarking large numbers of enslaved Africans each year, bound mainly for the Caribbean and the Americas, drawing the coastal kingdoms ever deeper into the Atlantic economy.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1700-peak-of-the-slave-trade-through-loango, claim TL:COG:event:1700:peak-of-the-slave-trade-through-loango, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Succession crisis weakens Loango
claims.summary: A succession crisis after the death of the king recorded as Buatu, together with the growing power of provincial governors and traders, undermined the maloango's central authority and began Loango's long decline.

sources.label: A history of the Loango kingdom (c. 1500–1883)

claims.title: Decline as the slave trade is suppressed
claims.summary: The European suppression of the Atlantic slave trade undercut the Loango coast's economy; the kingdom fragmented into small chieftaincies and had effectively ceased to exist as a unified state by the early 1880s.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1850-decline-as-the-slave-trade-is-suppressed, claim TL:COG:event:1850:decline-as-the-slave-trade-is-suppressed, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Brazza's treaty with Makoko
claims.summary: In September 1880 Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed a treaty with the Teke ruler Makoko Iloo I, placing his lands under French protection and securing France's claim to the north bank of the Congo River.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1880-brazza-s-treaty-with-makoko, claim TL:COG:event:1880:brazza-s-treaty-with-makoko, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Founding of Brazzaville at Nkuna
claims.summary: Brazza founded a French post at the village of Nkuna (Mfoa) on the north bank of Stanley Pool on 10 September 1880; held by Sergeant Malamine Camara, it was named Brazzaville and became the centre of French rule.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1880-founding-of-brazzaville-at-nkuna, claim TL:COG:event:1880:founding-of-brazzaville-at-nkuna, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Berlin Conference divides the two Congos
claims.summary: The Berlin Conference recognised French claims north of the Congo River and assigned the south bank to Leopold II's Congo Free State, fixing the lasting division between the Republic of the Congo and the future Democratic Republic.

claims.title: Middle Congo joins French Equatorial Africa
claims.summary: France reorganised its Central African colonies in 1910 into French Equatorial Africa — Gabon, Middle Congo, Ubangi-Shari and Chad — governed from Brazzaville, which became the federation's federal capital.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1910-middle-congo-joins-french-equatorial-africa, claim TL:COG:event:1910:middle-congo-joins-french-equatorial-africa, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Building the Congo-Ocean Railway
claims.summary: The Congo-Ocean Railway was built from 1921 to 1934 by the Société de Construction des Batignolles to link Brazzaville to Pointe-Noire; forced labourers conscripted across French Equatorial Africa died in the thousands, an estimate commonly placed above 17,000.

claims.title: Railway completed; Pointe-Noire opens as port
claims.summary: The roughly 512-kilometre railway was completed in 1934, establishing Pointe-Noire as the colony's Atlantic ocean terminal and the backbone of the export economy that bypassed the lower Congo rapids.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1934-railway-completed-pointe-noire-opens-as-port, claim TL:COG:event:1934:railway-completed-pointe-noire-opens-as-port, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Brazzaville, capital of Free France
claims.summary: After French Equatorial Africa rallied to General de Gaulle in 1940, Brazzaville became the effective capital of Free France, a base for organising resistance against Vichy and the Axis powers.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1940-brazzaville-capital-of-free-france, claim TL:COG:event:1940:brazzaville-capital-of-free-france, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: The Brazzaville Conference
claims.summary: De Gaulle convened the Brazzaville Conference in early 1944, which promised post-war colonial reforms — ending the harshest forced labour, granting African representation and citizenship — while explicitly rejecting independence.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1944-the-brazzaville-conference, claim TL:COG:event:1944:the-brazzaville-conference, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Autonomy within the French Community
claims.summary: Following the September 1958 referendum, Middle Congo became the autonomous Republic of the Congo within the French Community, a self-governing step short of full sovereignty.

claims.title: Independence under Fulbert Youlou
claims.summary: The Republic of the Congo became independent on 15 August 1960 with the Abbé Fulbert Youlou as its first president, a pro-Western leader who kept close ties to France.

claims.title: The Trois Glorieuses topple Youlou
claims.summary: A three-day popular uprising in August 1963, led by trade unions and youth, forced Youlou's resignation; Alphonse Massamba-Débat took power and steered the country toward one-party "scientific socialism."

claims.title: People's Republic of the Congo proclaimed
claims.summary: Marien Ngouabi, who had seized power in 1968, proclaimed the People's Republic of the Congo in 1969 — Africa's first Marxist-Leninist state — with the Congolese Labour Party (PCT) as the sole legal party.

claims.title: Assassination of Marien Ngouabi
claims.summary: President Marien Ngouabi was assassinated in Brazzaville on 18 March 1977; a military committee took power, and after a brief interim under General Yhombi-Opango leadership passed to Denis Sassou Nguesso in 1979.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1977-assassination-of-marien-ngouabi, claim TL:COG:event:1977:assassination-of-marien-ngouabi, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Sassou Nguesso takes power
claims.summary: Colonel Denis Sassou Nguesso became president in 1979, leading the PCT one-party state through the 1980s while petroleum became the mainstay of the economy and ties to France and Western oil firms deepened.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-1979-sassou-nguesso-takes-power, claim TL:COG:event:1979:sassou-nguesso-takes-power, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: National conference opens democracy
claims.summary: After the PCT dropped Marxism-Leninism in 1990, a sovereign national conference in 1991 stripped Sassou Nguesso of executive power, made him a ceremonial head of state and set the Congo on a path to multiparty elections.

claims.title: Lissouba wins multiparty election
claims.summary: Pascal Lissouba of UPADS won the Congo's first multiparty presidential election in August 1992, ending the PCT's monopoly and inaugurating a brief democratic period.

claims.title: Militia clashes over disputed elections
claims.summary: Disputes over the 1993 legislative elections sparked armed clashes between political militias in Brazzaville, fracturing the new democracy along factional and regional lines.

claims.title: Civil war returns Sassou Nguesso to power
claims.summary: Civil war erupted in June 1997 between forces of President Lissouba and former president Sassou Nguesso; backed by Angolan troops, Sassou Nguesso's forces prevailed by October, Lissouba fled into exile, and Sassou Nguesso declared himself president.

claims.title: New constitution; Sassou Nguesso elected
claims.summary: A new constitution adopted in 2002 entrenched Sassou Nguesso's presidency; he won the presidential election that year and was re-elected in 2009 amid opposition complaints.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Congo: From the Bantu peoples and the coastal Kingdom of Loango, through the Atlantic slave trade, Brazza's founding of Brazzaville and the colony of Middle Congo within French Equatorial Africa, to independence in 1960, the Marxist People's Republic, and the long rule of Denis Sassou Nguesso.", terralore.co/country/COG/chronicle#ev-2002-new-constitution-sassou-nguesso-elected, claim TL:COG:event:2002:new-constitution-sassou-nguesso-elected, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Referendum removes term limits
claims.summary: A constitutional referendum in October 2015, reported as overwhelmingly approved on a disputed turnout, scrapped presidential term limits and the age ceiling, clearing the way for Sassou Nguesso to seek further terms; he was re-elected in 2016 and 2021.
